ITP is the most common cause of isolated thrombocytopenia in otherwise healthy children and typically presents with acute onset of petechiae, bruising, and mucosal bleeding without systemic symptoms; high confidence reflects its epidemiologic dominance in this age group and clinical pattern. ALL is highly plausible due to bone marrow infiltration causing cytopenias—including thrombocytopenia—and may present with similar bleeding manifestations, often accompanied by fatigue, pallor, or low-grade fever (though not yet reported); its inclusion reflects urgent need to rule out malignancy. Aplastic anemia is less common but fits the bleeding phenotype due to pancytopenia; it warrants consideration especially if there’s no splenomegaly or lymphadenopathy and if anemia or neutropenia emerges on exam/lab. DIC is less likely in an otherwise stable child without sepsis, trauma, or malignancy triggers—but remains on the list given its potential for isolated early thrombocytopenia and microvascular bleeding. Bernard-Soulier syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive platelet adhesion defect causing lifelong mucocutaneous bleeding, but its presentation is usually chronic and often noted since infancy; absence of prior history and acute/subacute onset lowers its likelihood, hence lowest confidence."}

ALL must be urgently considered given its frequent presentation with cytopenias including thrombocytopenia, petechiae, and bleeding; bone marrow infiltration explains multisite hemorrhage and warrants high suspicion (0.82). DIC is plausible but less likely without documented systemic illness, sepsis, trauma, or malignancy—and absence of reported D-dimer/fibrinogen/PT/aPTT data lowers confidence (0.75). Fanconi anemia is a rare inherited bone marrow failure syndrome that can present in early childhood with thrombocytopenia and petechiae, often accompanied by subtle dysmorphic features or growth delay—moderately likely if additional clues emerge (0.62). Bernard-Soulier syndrome, a rare autosomal recessive platelet adhesion defect, causes mucocutaneous bleeding and thrombocytopenia but typically presents earlier (infancy) and with giant platelets; isolated bleeding without family history or macrothrombocytopenia on CBC makes it less probable (0.58). Diagnostic uncertainty reflects moderate dispersion across top diagnoses, consistent with overlapping phenotypes requiring targeted testing (CBC with smear, peripheral blood flow cytometry, bone marrow exam, genetic testing)."}
